Every evidence passage is checked verbatim against the downloaded source text by the build script. No ANTHROPIC or other paid API call.
thesis: The big US airlines sell their frequent flyer miles to banks that hand them to credit card holders. They book part of that money right away and defer the part owed as future flights until miles are redeemed, estimate how many miles will never be used, and have borrowed billions against these programs; because the airline sets the terms, it also controls what a mile is worth.
angle: Use the airlines' own 2025 filings to follow a mile from a grocery-store card swipe to the airline's books: who pays for it, how it is booked, how much is still owed, what lenders accepted as collateral in 2020, and why the government asked whether members get the value they were promised. A sequel to the gift-card film: the same idea of a balance the customer holds and the company forecasts.

contradictions.note: Card payments are not profit. Delta's $8.2 billion and American's $6.2 billion are cash for miles and other benefits; part is deferred as future flights. The script must not compare them with net income as if they were earnings, and must say 'paid' or 'cash', not 'profit'.

United's $21.9 billion is United's own figure (12 times MileagePlus 2019 EBITDA), stated in its 8-K, not an independent appraisal or a market value. The script must attribute it to United and describe the method.
American's 2024 cash payments included a one-time payment for a new card agreement, so the 2024-to-2025 change is not a clean growth rate. Do not compute or imply growth for American.
The DOT inquiry (September 2024) is an inquiry, not a finding. No outcome has been verified; the script must not claim any penalty, ruling or confirmed devaluation.
Miles do not simply 'never expire': American's miles stay valid only with qualifying activity every 24 months or for a primary co-branded cardholder. Only state what each filing says.

claims.text: Delta reported that remuneration from American Express related to the SkyMiles program was $8.2 billion in 2025, about 11% more than in 2024, and said it expects that remuneration to grow to $10 billion over the next few years.

evidence.passage: Remuneration from American Express related to the SkyMiles program were $8.2 billion during 2025, an increase of approximately 11% compared to 2024.
In 2025, remuneration from American Express totaled $8.2 billion, which we expect to grow to $10 billion over the next few years.

scope.note: Remuneration is cash paid for miles and other benefits, not profit; the $10 billion is Delta's own expectation, not a fact.

claims.text: Delta sells SkyMiles to American Express, which gives them to its cardholders; customers also earn miles by spending with credit card, retail, ridesharing, car rental and hotel partners, which pay Delta monthly based on the miles sold.

evidence.passage: We sell miles to American Express which are then provided to their customers under the co-brand credit card program and the Membership Rewards program.

Customers earn miles based on their spending with participating companies such as credit card, retail, ridesharing, car rental and hotel companies with which we have marketing agreements to sell miles. Payments are typically due to us monthly based on the volume of miles sold during the period.

claims.text: Delta splits what American Express pays across what it delivers (award travel, baggage fee waivers, lounge access, priority boarding and the use of its brand); the part allocated to award travel is deferred and only becomes passenger revenue when miles are redeemed and the flight is provided.

evidence.passage: We allocate the value based on the relative selling prices of those products and services, which generally consist of award travel, baggage fee waivers, lounge access, priority boarding and the use of our brand.

We defer the amount allocated to award travel as part of loyalty program deferred revenue and recognize loyalty travel awards in passenger revenue as the miles are redeemed and transportation is provided.

claims.text: American estimates with a statistical model how many AAdvantage miles will never be redeemed and recognizes that value as other miles are redeemed; a 10% higher estimate of unredeemed miles would have raised 2025 revenue by about $140 million. Its miles generally do not expire with qualifying activity at least every 24 months or for a primary co-branded cardholder.

evidence.passage: For the portion of our outstanding mileage credits that we estimate will not be redeemed, we recognize the associated value proportionally as the remaining mileage credits are redeemed. Our estimates use a statistical model based on historical redemption patterns to develop an estimate of the likelihood of future redemption. For the year ended December 31, 2025, a hypothetical 10% increase in our estimate of mileage credits not expected to be redeemed would have increased revenues by approximately $140 million.

Mileage credits can be redeemed at any time and generally do not expire as long as the AAdvantage member has any type of qualifying activity at least every 24 months or if the AAdvantage member is the primary holder of a co-branded credit card.

inferences.text: Our arithmetic: Delta's SkyMiles deferred revenue grew by $436 million in 2025 ($9,262 million less $8,826 million): more miles were issued than redeemed.

Our arithmetic: at the end of 2025, American's liability for unredeemed miles ($10,564 million) was $3,406 million larger than its liability for tickets already sold for future flights ($7,158 million).
Our arithmetic: United's frequent flyer deferred revenue at December 31, 2025 totals $7,777 million ($3,721 million current plus $4,056 million noncurrent).
Our arithmetic: the three airlines' balances for miles not yet redeemed at December 31, 2025 add up to about $27.6 billion ($9,262 million Delta, $10,564 million American, $7,777 million United).
Our arithmetic: United's $21.9 billion figure implies MileagePlus 2019 EBITDA of about $1.8 billion ($21.9 billion divided by 12).

Rounded to one decimal place in billions: American's loyalty program liability is about $10.6 billion and its air traffic liability about $7.2 billion, a gap of about $3.4 billion; United's frequent flyer deferred revenue is about $7.8 billion.
